analysis.one_liner: Requires clear disclosure, consent, and easy cancellation for subscription and auto-renewal charges.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote; it died when the 117th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted 'negative option' sales — subscriptions, free trials that convert to paid plans, and clubs that keep shipping until you say stop. It would have banned charging a consumer unless the seller clearly disclosed all terms, got the consumer's explicit yes, and provided a way to cancel through the same channel used to sign up. It also required advance notice before automatic renewals and price jumps after a free or cheap trial. Enforcement would have come through the Federal Trade Commission and state attorneys general.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who sign up for free trials, streaming services, gym memberships, subscription boxes, or continuity clubs and then keep getting charged because cancellation is buried or requires a phone call during business hours. Anyone who has paid for months for a service they meant to cancel gains the right to cancel the way they signed up, plus warnings before renewals and price increases.

how_it_helps.text: It would be illegal to charge a consumer through a negative option unless the seller clearly and conspicuously disclosed all material terms before taking billing information or payment.
Sellers would need the consumer's express informed consent before charging, and could not auto-renew for more than a month after an introductory period without fresh consent.

Every negative option agreement would have to include a simple cancellation mechanism, including the ability to cancel the same way the consumer signed up — for example, canceling online if you subscribed online.

For free-to-pay conversion contracts, sellers would have to warn consumers before the first full charge, state the upcoming cost and price increase, and send regular reminders with cancellation information; automatic renewal contracts require notice 2 to 7 days before the initial renewal and at least annual reminders.
The FTC could enforce the rules as unfair or deceptive practices, and state attorneys general could sue in federal court on behalf of their residents.

analysis.who_pays: Companies that rely on automatic renewals and hard-to-cancel subscriptions bear the cost: building cancellation flows, sending reminders, and losing revenue from subscribers who forget or fail to cancel. That includes streaming services, gyms, subscription boxes, and marketers of free trials that convert to paid plans.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs fall on businesses of every size, including small sellers of subscription goods, who must build consent flows, reminder systems, and same-channel cancellation for every plan.

The bill preempts state laws only where they directly conflict, but a single federal floor could replace a patchwork of stricter state auto-renewal rules for practices the federal standard covers less strictly.
Requiring consent before every renewal longer than one month could disrupt legitimate subscription models, such as annual plans, that consumers actively want to keep.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer benefit is direct and easy to state: fewer surprise charges and cancellations as easy as sign-ups. The costs are real but modest — reminder notices, consent clicks, and cancellation links — and fall on the businesses that currently profit from inertia. The bill is a straightforward consumer protection with limited downside for consumers themselves.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, and it died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Brian Schatz introduced the Unsubscribe Act of 2021 on June 16, 2021, joined by Republican Senators Thune and Kennedy and Democrat Warnock as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation the same day.
The bill attracted three cosponsors — two Republicans and one Democrat — but no further action was ever taken.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, without the committee reporting the bill or the Senate voting on it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Subscription businesses that profit from automatic renewals, free trials that convert to paid plans, and hard-to-cancel flows are better off, because they keep charging consumers under the old rules. Consumers who wanted an easy unsubscribe got nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Subscription businesses keeping the status quo

for.name: Sen. Brian Schatz
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (chair: Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-WA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled a markup or sent it to the floor during the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan from the start — a Democrat leading with two Republicans and one additional Democrat cosponsoring — so the bill's death was not a party-line vote but a committee that never acted.

industries.industry: Subscription and auto-renewal businesses (streaming, gyms, subscription boxes, continuity plans)
industries.note: These companies profit when consumers forget to cancel or face obstacles to canceling. The bill would force disclosure, consent, same-channel cancellation, and renewal reminders, cutting revenue from inactive subscribers.

Businesses built on cheap or free introductory offers that convert to full-price billing would need explicit consent before each conversion and warnings before the first full charge, shrinking the value of silent conversions.
Card networks and payment processors would face demands for simpler recurring-payment cancellation tools, but clearer consent records could also reduce chargeback disputes that cost them money.
